# 1. Business data

The accompanying file `BusinessData.csv` contains data on the number of businesses in each constituency in England, as well as a variety of social and demographic measurements. The goal of this question is to construct a linear model with the number of businesses as the response. We will treat all covariates and the response as real-valued (rather than integer-valued) for simplicity.

First, load the data and restrict it to the subset of covariates that will be the focus of this question.^[Here, `dep` indicates a measure related to a deprivation index.]

```{r}
BusinessData <- read.csv("BusinessData.csv")

BusinessData <- BusinessData[,c("Businesses","TotalPopulation2011","prop_village_or_smaller",
                                "Median_wage_2017","Pop0_15Age","Pop16_64Age",
                                "Prop_born_in_UK_2011","Health_dep",
                                "LivingEnvironment_dep","Education_dep",
                                "Employment_dep")]
```

(a) Fit a linear model to predict the number of businesses in each constituency using all ten covariates. Plot the predicted against the actual number of businesses in each constituency. \hfill [3 marks]

(b) Compute the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), and mean squared error from leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) associated with this model. For AIC and BIC you may use built-in functions, but you should make clear what formula each function computes and the value of any input parameters for this dataset. \hfill [4 marks]

(c) It is suggested that this model is unnecessarily complicated and that one might find a simpler model with similar performance by discarding one or more covariates. For each covariate, construct a linear model to predict the number of businesses with that covariate removed. According to AIC, do you find a better model? \hfill [4 marks]

(d) Starting from the best model with nine covariates, repeat the procedure in part (c), each time removing the single covariate that leads to a model producing the best available AIC for a model of that size. Continue down to the intercept-only model so that you can examine the complete sequence of nested models^[This method is known as *greedy backward stepwise selection*. In a conventional early-stopping implementation, one would stop as soon as no deletion improved AIC.]. Plot AIC as a function of the number of covariates included. Which model do you recommend overall? \hfill [6 marks]

(e) Repeat parts (c) and (d) using BIC and LOOCV instead of AIC. Compare the three methods. \hfill [4 marks]

(f) The plot of mean square error produced by LOOCV against the number of covariates can be regarded as an approximation to the test error of each model. Add the empirical *training* error to your plot. Comment on your results in the context of under- and over-fitting. \hfill [4 marks]
